However, in the long run, it is undeniably harmful to American economic interests. It makes American students - trained and familiar in Imperial but not in Metric - less desirable to companies that work on international projects. It reduces capacity for trade in that entirely different product specifications have to be made for American products (screws in particular) as opposed to having a mass-producible standard, and reduces cross-industry applications since it's harder to make compatible products - an assembly line tooled for metric-scale products can't effectively make imperial-scale products (again, screws and drills are a HUGE part of this). The implications are subtle, but far-reaching and damaging in the long term.

It's very much above the head of the common individual - the effect in day to day life might mean a cent or two more on certain products and whatnot - but it's the long run that needs to be played.

No. Please hear out my reasoning:

There are significant difficulties in dividing evenly within the metric system. You are always left with ridiculous long decimals that don't give you any perspective of scale and further cause massive confusion. One of these famous flaws in the decimal system's representation of numbers regards divisibility by 3, which has lead to the notion that ".9999999~ = 1". This flaw is not present in many other bases, and is commonly discussed because dividing by 3 is difficult when you are using decimal numbers.

For instance, even factors of 10 are 1, 2, 5, and 10.
Even factors of base 12 (inches) are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, and 12.
12 inches is a foot, 3 feet (36 inches) is a yard. That is the most common conversion.
For measurements smaller than an inch, you simply divide by 16, which has even factors of 1, 2, 4, 8, and 16. If you need to get smaller, you double the bottom part of the fraction to effectively change the base from 16 to 32, then 64, etc. This is extremely useful because it's the logical expansion of base 2, and base 8 is commonly used when learning computing concepts like subnetting.
If you wanted to measure large distances (unfortunately in base 10), you can remember that a mile is 5280 feet, and that 5280 / 3 = 1760, and there are 1760 yards in a mile.

Is the Imperial system perfect? Absolutely not, in fact its pretty awful and in many cases the metric system is superior, but you use different tools for different jobs, and I don't think the metric system is qualified to call itself a one-size-fits-all solution. It is absolutely worth recognizing that the metric system is just as arbitrary as the imperial system, and that for some applications the metric system is not as useful as the imperial system.

Base 60 is used to measure time, geographic coordinates, and angles - yet not even the staunchest metric system zealot advocates for eliminating those and replacing them with a base 10 system. There is no need to dictate to people what they ought to use.
